Make a document beside the node; whoever makes one owns it.
Discuss a document: start a discussion, answer in one, react and resolve.
Manage the documents beside the node, or this document: put an earlier version back, move it, delete and restore it, and delete anybody's comment.
See the thread and read its conversation, its state and its usage; follow it.
Drive the agent: give it input, steer or interrupt a running turn, stop or retry one, put in order what waits, and set the thread's tags.
Set the session up: its name, model and effort, the agent's parameters and instructions, its approval mode, its provider and profile; answer what the agent asks; delete the thread.
Take a fork of the thread: a new thread of one's own, with as much of its history as one chooses.
Archive the thread, and bring it back.

Start threads in the topic, announce to its threads, set its status and tags, and create an environment for work there.
Rename the topic, change its description, its parameters and its default environment, delete it, and restore what was deleted in it.
Archive the topic, and bring it back.
Start threads in the topic; whoever starts one owns it.
See the project: its name, description and the settings that are no secret, and who has access.
Create topics, announce to the open topics of the project, set its tags, and create an environment for work there.
Rename the project, change its description and parameters, move it to another org of its tree, delete it, and restore what was deleted in it.
Archive the project, and bring it back.
Create topics in the project; whoever creates one owns it.
See the org: its name, its members and groups, the orgs inside it and the settings that are no secret.
Create projects, announce to the open topics of the org, set its tags, and create an environment for work there.
Rename the org, change its parameters and tags, create orgs inside it, move it within its tree, delete it, and restore what was deleted in it.
Archive the org with everything inside it, and bring it back.
Write the policies and locks of the node, its secrets, and where what happens there is sent.
Read every record of use in the node and below it, and the caps defined there.
See how much was used in the node as figures by person, model, provider, agent and kind of environment, without anybody else's records.
Add, change and remove the usage caps of the node.
Let one turn run past a cap that is defined on the node and has no room left.
Read the audit trail of the node and of what is inside it.
Invite people into the org, remove, suspend and move them, and manage its groups and service accounts.
Read the direct and group chats among the org's members without being in them.
Change who holds what on the thing, and on a place also its defaults and its roles; decide requests for access; share it with agents.
Be one of its owners: hold everything on its page, and say who else owns it and who else may change the page.

Take the chat of the node away as a file: its own export, its place in an archive, a copy given to an agent, and an agent's download of it.
Take the documents beside the node, or this document, away as files: its own export, its place in an archive, a copy given to an agent, and an agent's download of it.

Change the profile and its overrides, and enable, disable and delete it.

Start threads in the environment, and have the agents of its threads act for oneself there: give them input, steer or interrupt their turns, stop or retry one.
Have all of the environment: where its threads run, how far agents are confined and what it offers; start, stop, recreate, update, configure, move and remove it.

Change the files of that workspace through Orch, and make, label and restore snapshots.
See the processes of the environment and what they use, and watch an agent's own terminal there.
Open a shell of one's own in the environment and come back to it, signal processes there, and type into an agent's own terminal.
See the browsers open in the environment and the profiles it keeps, and watch a tab of one, and who else watches or drives it.
Drive a browser of the environment with pointer and keys, open and close its tabs, open or quit one, make, rename and delete profiles, and read the address a browser is driven at.
See the displays served in the environment, and watch one.
Work in a display with pointer, keys and the clipboard, open one from a preset, and close one.

Read callers and both ends, admit a named place, link or host within current policy, and close openings or decide port requests.

Have environments and a provider's runtime made on the host, or moved to it, within what the entry allows.
